newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas trade officials labor on FTAA groundwork.
newsitem.headline: Americas trade officials labor on FTAA groundwork.

text.p: Deputy trade ministers from 34 countries in the Americas were laboriously laying the groundwork for negotiating a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) in a meeting in Rio de Janeiro, officials said.

"I would say today's meeting has been very positive. We are on the path of gradual approximation," said Jose Botafogo Goncalves, general subsecretary of economic integration and international trade at the Brazilian Foreign Ministry.

Officials from the 34 signatory countries of the FTAA, which according to a 1994 Miami summit agreement is supposed to come into force by 2005, were meeting in Rio de Janeiro for final talks before a May 15-16 ministerial summit in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte.
The Rio talks, which began Monday evening and go on till Thursday, are expected to produce a Ministerial Declaration for Belo Horizonte.
Botafogo acknowledged that differences remained considerable, especially over the timetable for negotiations.

Canadian officials, requesting anonymity, said virtually all parties except the Mercosur trade bloc, which groups Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, had lined up behind an American proposal to start discussing all aspects of trade liberalization at the same time.

Mercosur has stuck to its position that talks should begin on "business facilitation", basically the eradication of bureaucratic barriers to trade, then move on to subsidies before focusing on the thorny issue of tariff reductions.

Jorge Campbell, secretary of international economic relations at the Argentine Foreign Ministry, said all countries agreed to stick by the FTAA dream and start formal negotiations after a presidential FTAA summit in Santiago, Chile, next year.

They also agreed on the need to define now "what work remains to be done" by Santiago for the free trade talks to be effective. He said a further ministerial meeting, to be held in Costa Rica, would precede Santiago.
"What we want to define is the path (to Santiago)," Campbell told reporters at a joint briefing with Botafogo. "The differences we have are not irreconcilable."
The Canadians suggested too that some approximation between the two conflicting positions might be forthcoming.

"(In trade talks) everyone's busy sharpening pencils and doing homework at first," one said, referring to the fact that the initial stages of trade talks do not necessarily require concrete decisions.
Brazil Wednesday presented to the delegates in Rio a condensed memo of 16 paragraphs, listing all subjects agreed on and disagreed on.
Botafogo said he expected "deep" discussion to take place in the afternoon.

Delegates said a spat between Argentina and the United States, which Tuesday withdrew trade benefits in retaliation for "inadequate" intellectual property rights, had not affected the atmosphere of the FTAA meeting.
"Zero, absolutely zero," said Campbell when questioned about the impact of the issue.
